gap: No result ChatGPT got states that only the EPO (auto-shutoff) Power Watchdog Gen II has a disconnect that can cut or restore the RV's power, remotely too. It trips below 104 V or above 132 V and reconnects only after 90 seconds of stable power. The household plug ChatGPT also showed (Kasa EP40) is limited to 15 A / 1,875 W in total across both outlets and needs a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network, against the 30 A / 3,600 W of an RV shore connection.
standout_why: Compared against the pages ChatGPT got. rvupgradestore.com's PWD30EPOW listing (cited) already gives the 104 V / 132 V cutoff, 30 A / 3,600 W and a bare 'Remote Power Control' callout, so part of the finding is already there. Its result titles also separate 'with Auto Shutoff' models from plain ones. The two cited hughesautoformers.com URLs now 301-redirect to powerwatchdog.com, which could not be opened (certificate error). No result page states the 90-second reconnect delay. None says in plain words that you can 'cut or restore power to your RV remotely' only on the EPO unit. None gives the Kasa EP40's 15 A-in-total / 1,875 W limit or its 2.4 GHz-only Wi-Fi requirement, though ChatGPT's own answer warned in general terms against household plugs on shore power.
decides: If the shopper wants a 'smart plug' that can switch the whole RV off and on from a phone, the pick has to be an EPO model (PWD30EPOW / PWD50EPOW), because that is where the remote cut/restore and auto-shutoff are described. The non-EPO PWD30W / PWD50W listings describe only monitoring, alerts and surge absorption. ChatGPT's $169.99 'Gen II 30A' card therefore may not switch anything. A Kasa EP40 or Minoston MP22Z only fits single 120 V loads under 15 A inside the coach. The Kasa also needs a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi network in the RV, and the Minoston needs a Z-Wave hub (retailer listings only).
